div.p: Real-tame expert systems are embedded decision systems which must respond to changes in the environments within stringent timing constraints. Given a program p , the response time analysis problem is to determine the maximal response time of p .

In this paper, we tackle this problem with a response tame upper bound algorithm for a class of EQL rulebased programs whose variables range over finite do- mains. This algorithm computes a response time upper bound of the given program by determining the maximal number of rule firings which result from the firings of individual rules enabled at the invocation.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time expert systems are embedded decision systems which must respond to changes in the environments within stringent timing constraints. A major problem impeding the use of rule-based expert systems in real-time monitoring and control environments is t,he difficulty in predicting the response time of these rule-based systems. Given a program p , the response time analysis problem is to determine the maximal re- sponse time of p . It has been proved [14] that the response time analysis problem is undecidable if program variables have infinite domains, and is PSPACE hard in the case where all of the variables have finite domains. In this paper, we tackle this problem with a response time upper bound algorithm for a class of EQL rule-based programs with the property that each rule is either enabled or disabled throughout execution, but the values assigned to variables by each rule are not constant.

Real-time systems have received their share of attention in recent years. However, few attempts have been made to formally address the response time analysis problem. Lark et a1 [13] consider the design and implementation issues in the development of the Lockheed Pilot's Associate system. They advocate using experimentation and analysis to guarantee timeliness by requiring the application programmer to set an upper bound on process duration by extensive experimentation but do not show how to verify that the system will satisfy this upper bound. Aiken et a1 [3] presents a static analysis method for determining whether arbitrary sets of database production rules satisfy certain properties, including termination. A directed graph demonstrating the triggering relationship among rules are checked to see if the corresponding set of rules is guaranteed to terminate. Some conditions that guarantee the property of termination are introduced. However, they do not provide an algorithm for obtaining an execution time (or execution time upper bound) for a set of rules which is found to have the property of termination. Abiteboul and Simon [l] discuss, among others, the property of termination in the context of Datalog and its extensions and show that this property is in general undecidable. Although they address the issue of whether all programs of a given language possess the property of termination, the issue of determining whether a given program possesses the property of termination is not addressed.

div.head: Previous results
div.p: The EQuational Logic (EQL) [4] language is a simple language designed as a model-investigation language to develop techniques to obtain the response time of real-time rule-based programs. Browne et a1 [4] report a set of analysis tools to determine the response times of EQL programs. This set of tools relies mainly on a temporal logic model checker based on the Clarke-Emerson-Sistla algorithm [9] and a timing analyzer that conducts an exhaustive depth-first search on the state space graph to determine the maximal number of rule firings for the given program to reach a tixed point. Due to the exhaustive nature of state space graph checks, it may take a long time for these tools to conduct an analysis even on a small program.
To remedy this problem, the General Analysis Algorzthm [7] is used to partition the analyzed program such that only a small part of the program is analyzed at a time.

Furthermore, there are sets, each of which is called a Special Form, of syntactic and semantic constraint assertions with the property that the execution of a set of rules always terminates in bounded time if this set of rules satisfies a Special Form. Cheng [6] reports a Daffusaon-of-Num6ers algorithm to compute response time upper bounds for programs satisfying some Special Forms. This algorithm computes the numbers of changes of program variables as a basis to determine an upper bound on the number of rule firings. Cheng and Chen [8] introduce a Back-Tracking algorithm to analyze a class of EQL programs. This algorithm takes a backward approach to compute the maximal number of times that a rule can be fired during the execution by determining all of the possible firing sequences resulting i n the tiring of the particular rule considered.

However, these algorithms do not fully exploit the characteristics of Special Forms. In this paper, we present a new algorithm exploiting the characteristics of Special Form to determine tighter response time upper bounds. This new algorithm takes a forward approach by determining, for each rule T , the set of rules which can possibly be fired as a result of the firing of T. It also exploits the property of mutual exclusiveness among rules to tighten upper bounds.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly explains the syntax and the semantics of the EQuational Logic language. The general strategy used to analyze EQL programs is also outlined in this section. In Section 3, we present the new algorithm used to obtain response time upper bounds for a class of EQL programs. Finally, Section 4 concludes this paper.

div.head: The EQuational Logic language
div.p: An EQL program has a set of rules for updating variables which denote the state of the physical system under control. Every time sensor readings are taken, the variables are recomputed iteratively by a number of rule firings until no further change in the variables can result from the firing of a rule. The EQL program is then said t o have reached a fixed point'.

div.head: The syntax of EQL
div.p: Let p denote an EQL program. p consists of a finite set of rules and a finite set of variables denoting the state of the system. The set of variables is called the state variable, which consists of two parts: input variables and non-input variables. The values of input variables are obtained through sensor readings sampled periodically, while non-input variables receive new values as a result of rule firings.

For each rule r in p , r is a conditional statement of the form a1 := bl I . . . 1 0 d := bd IF EC where d 2 1 and the symbol ' 1' stands for AND. If bi does not contain a non-input variable, the assignment ai := bi is a constant-expression assignment; otherwise, it is a variable-expression assignment. EC is a predicate on the program variables and is called the Enabling Condition. div.head: High-Level Dependency graph
div.p: A High-Level Dependency (HLD) graph is a directed graph which shows the dependency among sets of rules and is the basis to assign priorities to rules. Each of the vertices in the HLD graph represents a set of rule(s) and is called a forward-independent set. If the set S and the set SI do not satisfy the condition L S I n ( L s U Rs U Ts) = 0, then the corresponding HLD graph includes a directed edge from the vertex representing S to the vertex representing S I , meaning that S may not be independent of SI, and the rules in S are assigned lower priorities than the rules in SI. Rules in the same forward-independent set are assigned the same priority. A High-Level Dependency graph construction procedure was reported in [7]. For more details about this procedure, please refer to [7].

Figure 1 shows a sample HLD graph. There is a directed edge from C2 to Cl, meaning that C2 is not independent of C1. Hence, the rules 1 and 2 are assigned higher priorities than the rules 3 and 4, which in turn are assigned higher priorities than the rules 8 and 9, and so on. Note that the rules 3 and 4 may be assigned the same priority as the rules 5, 6, and 7.

div.head: Special Form
div.p: A Special Form is a set of syntactic and semantic constraint assertions such that if a set of rules satisfies all of these assertions, then the execution of this set of rules always terminates in bounded time. Hence, to check if the execution of a set of rules always terminates in bounded time, we can first check if this set of rules satisfies any Special Form. If yes, then a response time upper bound can be obtained by executing the corresponding response time upper bound algorithm; otherwise, the aforementioned model checker and timing analyzer need to be used to determine a response time upper bound.

The Special Form discussed in this paper is called Special Form C [6]. We will also present an algorithm, namely Algorithm-C, used to compute response time upper bound of programs satisfying Special Form C. First, some definitions are in order.

div.head: Algorithm-C
div.p: Assume p is an n-rule Special Form C program. The execution of p is a sequence of rule firings, which can be regarded as a series of subsequences of rule firings. Each subsequence of rule firings starts with the firing of some rule which is firable at the invocation (i.e. , we say this rule initiates a subsequence of rule firings during the execution of p . ) According to Theorem 3.1, p always reaches a fixed point in a bounded number of rule firings. This means that the firing of one rule can result in at most a bounded number of rule firings. Hence, each subsequence consists of up to a bounded number of rule firings. The number of rule firings during the execution of p is equal to the sum of the numbers of rule firings in individual subsequences.

For each rule r E p , r can be firable because (1) the state at the invocation makes r firable, or (2) the firing of some rule, say r', makes r firable. Due to C2, if a rule is enabled/disabled at the invocation, then it remains enabled/disabled throughout the execution of p . This means that only rules which are enabled at the invocation can possibly be firable during the execution of p . Hence, if a firing of r' makes r firable, it must be due to the fact that this firing of r' changes the value of a variable in R, (and r is enabled at the invocation). The emphasis of this paper is on determining response time upper bounds for a class of real-time rule-based systems. In general, the amount of time needed to analyze real-time rule-based systems to predict their response time is usually large. In this paper, we tackle this problem with a response time analysis algorithm based on a simple syntactic and semantic check on programs. The concept of Special Form is exploited. A class of EQL real-time rule-based programs, with the property that each rule is either enabled or disabled throughout each execution and the values as-+net1 to variables by each rule are not constant, is investigated. This new algorithm shows significant improvement over the Back-Tracking approach [8] in terms of the tightness of the upper bounds obtained.

By using the Special Form approach, we have successfully reduced the time needed in analyzing some real-life real-time rule-based systems. For example, to analyze the Cryogenic Hydrogen Pressure Malfunction Procedure of the Space Shuttle Vehicle (SSV) Pressure Control System [12], it took two weeks of time for a set of tools relying mainly on an exhaustive state space graph check to complete the analysis. However, it is verified by GAA that this program can be partitioned into forward independent subsets such that each of these subsets is in a known Special Form. This fact contributes to the huge reduction in the time needed from two weeks to two seconds for a set of tools employing GAA equipped with Special Form to complete the analysis.

Currently, we are attempting to generalize the proposed algorithm. The preliminary result shows that this algorithm can be applied to a larger class of programs than the class of Special Form C programs. We also plan to investigate the response time analysis of more expressive rule-based languages such as OPS5 [lo] which allows the use of structured variables.
